questions.q: Warm-up: a database migration is a project with an end. Which job instead keeps a second copy up to date with no planned end date?
options: Cutting over to the new database
Replication
Moving one table at a time
Converting the structure
questions.explain: Replication keeps a second copy current until you decide to stop. A migration is a project that ends when you switch the app to the new database.

questions.q: Your team moves from Oracle to PostgreSQL, so the database technology itself changes. Why is that harder than moving between two databases of the same kind?
options: The data has to be copied twice
Table definitions, data types and stored code all have to be converted
The old database has to be switched off first
It always needs a long outage
questions.explain: A move that changes the technology is called heterogeneous. Everything that describes the data has to be converted, not just the rows, so it takes more care than a same-engine move.

questions.q: Can a migration have truly zero downtime for the people using the app?
options: Yes, if you copy the data slowly enough
No, but you can aim for a pause so short nobody notices
Yes, but only when moving between clouds
No, you always need a full day offline
questions.explain: Nobody can promise zero downtime. Google's own architecture guide says truly zero downtime is impossible, so aim for near-zero: copy first, catch up on changes, then switch in a short pause.

questions.q: The copy tool finished and reported no errors. What should you do next?
options: Switch over right away, since no errors means it is right
Delete the old database to avoid confusion
Nothing, validation only matters for one-time moves
Check the copy anyway: it should be complete, free of duplicates and in the right order
questions.explain: "It copied without errors" is not the same as "it's right." A good copy is complete, has no duplicates and keeps things in order, so check before you switch.

questions.q: The app is now running on the new database. What is the safest thing to do with the old one?
options: Keep it as a fallback until the new one has proven reliable
Delete it the same day to save money
Keep using it for new writes as well
Archive it and stop watching the new one
questions.explain: Resist deleting the old database that day. Keeping it gives you a way back if something unexpected shows up, and you delete it once the new one runs reliably.
